a concise summary of what’s in the project.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## 1. Project structure\\\\n\\\\n**Top-level (project root):**\\\\n- **Assets/** – main content\\\\n- **Library/** – Unity cache/build artifacts\\\\n- **Logs/** – Unity logs\\\\n- **ProjectSettings/** – project and XR settings\\\\n- **UserSettings/** – editor layouts\\\\n- **Packages/** – package manifest (XR packages listed below)\\\\n\\\\n**Under &#96;Assets/&#96;:**\\\\n- **scripts/** – your C# scripts (3 files)\\\\n- **Scenes/** – includes &#96;escape_room.unity&#96; (main VR scene)\\\\n- **XR/** – OpenXR package settings\\\\n- **XRI/** – XR Interaction Toolkit settings (e.g. &#96;InteractionLayerSettings.asset&#96;)\\\\n- **VNB - Office Set/** – office asset pack: Prefabs/Office, Prefabs/Furniture, Scenes, Textures, Materials, ReadMe\\\\n- **Office Pack/** – office pack: Prefabs (Computers, Chairs, Clocks), Models, Demo.unity\\\\n- **SocketsAndSwitches/** – socket/switch asset pack (materials, prefabs; no C# in Assets)\\\\n- **Samples/** – XR Interaction Toolkit 3.3.1, XR Hands 1.7.3, OpenXR Plugin 1.16.1 (Starter Assets, Hands Interaction Demo, Controller samples)\\\\n- **school/** – school props and prefabs (chairs, etc.)\\\\n- **ADI/** – Voxel Office Props (chairs, etc.)\\\\n- **3d Objects/Office Chair Pack 1.0/** – office chair prefabs and demo scene\\\\n- **PolyKebap/** – LED Light Essentials Pack\\\\n- **TextMesh Pro/** – TMP shaders/resources\\\\n- **TutorialInfo/** – readme scripts\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## 2. VR framework / SDK\\\\n\\\\nThe project uses **Unity’s XR stack** (no Oculus SDK or SteamVR packages):\\\\n\\\\n- **XR Interaction Toolkit (XRI)** – &#96;com.unity.xr.interaction.toolkit&#96; **3.3.1**  \\\\n  - Used for interaction (grab, ray, teleport, locomotion, UI).\\\\n- **OpenXR** – &#96;com.unity.xr.openxr&#96; **1.16.1**  \\\\n  - Runtime layer; supports Oculus/Meta Quest, Microsoft Motion Controller, Valve Index, HTC Vive, etc. via OpenXR.\\\\n- **XR Hands** – &#96;com.unity.xr.hands&#96; **1.7.3**  \\\\n  - Hand tracking / hand visualization.\\\\n\\\\nSo: **XR Interaction Toolkit + OpenXR** (and XR Hands). No separate Oculus SDK or SteamVR; Quest and others are targeted through OpenXR.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## 3. Scripts for interaction, grabbing, puzzle mechanics\\\\n\\\\n**Your scripts in &#96;Assets/scripts/&#96;:**\\\\n\\\\n| Script               | Purpose |\\\\n|----------------------|--------|\\\\n| **notebookhand.cs**  | Class &#96;HandSpecificGrabPoints&#96;. Requires &#96;XRGrabInteractable&#96;; on select, detects left/right hand (via interactor name) and sets &#96;attachTransform&#96; to &#96;leftHandAttach&#96; or &#96;rightHandAttach&#96;. Used in &#96;escape_room.unity&#96;. |\\\\n| **AnimateHandOnInput.cs** | Drives a hand &#96;Animator&#96; from &#96;InputActionProperty&#96; trigger and grip (float → “Trigger” and “Grip” parameters). |\\\\n| **lightswitch.cs**    | Class &#96;PokeToggle&#96;. Toggles two groups (e.g. lights on/off and switch on/off) with cooldown; has &#96;OnPoke()&#96; for poke interaction. Used in &#96;escape_room.unity&#96; on &#96;lightswitch_poke&#96; with &#96;PokeToggle&#96;. |\\\\n\\\\n**XR Interaction Toolkit samples (in &#96;Assets/Samples/&#96;):**  \\\\nInteraction/grab-related samples include: &#96;RotationAxisLockGrabTransformer&#96;, &#96;ControllerInputActionManager&#96;, &#96;ObjectSpawner&#96;, &#96;XRPokeFollowAffordance&#96;, &#96;ToggleComponentZone&#96;, teleport/climb scripts, and Hands Interaction Demo scripts (e.g. &#96;PokeGestureDetector&#96;, &#96;PinchPointFollow&#96;). Great, now I have a solid understanding of your project. You're using **XR Interaction Toolkit 3.3.1 + OpenXR**, and you already have grab interaction experience (`HandSpecificGrabPoints` on the notebook) and a poke-based puzzle (`PokeToggle` light switch). There's no existing code lock or chair puzzle logic, so this would be built from scratch.

Here's a full breakdown of how to implement this feature:

---

## Architecture Overview

You'll need **3 scripts** and some scene setup:

| Script | Role |
|--------|------|
| `GrabbableChair.cs` | Makes a chair grabbable and constrains its movement to slide along one axis (back/forth from desk) |
| `ChairSlot.cs` | A snap zone at each desk that detects which chair is currently docked |
| `ChairPuzzleManager.cs` | Checks the arrangement of all chairs against the correct order and triggers unlock |

---

## 1. Making Chairs Grabbable (Constrained Movement)

Each chair needs:
- A **Rigidbody** (set to `isKinematic = false`, `useGravity = true`)
- An **`XRGrabInteractable`** component (from XR Interaction Toolkit)
- Movement constrained to **one axis** (e.g., Z-axis — sliding toward/away from the desk)

Since you're on XRI 3.3.1, you can constrain movement using Rigidbody constraints or a custom **XRGrabTransformer**. The simplest approach is to freeze the axes you don't want:

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.Interaction.Toolkit;
using UnityEngine.XR.Interaction.Toolkit.Interactables;

[RequireComponent(typeof(XRGrabInteractable))]
[RequireComponent(typeof(Rigidbody))]
public class GrabbableChair : MonoBehaviour
{
    [Header("Chair Identity")]
    [Tooltip("Unique ID for this chair (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4)")]
    public int chairID;

    [Header("Slide Constraint")]
    [Tooltip("Local axis to allow sliding along (e.g. 0,0,1 for Z)")]
    public Vector3 slideAxis = Vector3.forward;

    [Tooltip("Min/max distance from the desk along the slide axis")]
    public float minSlide = -1f;
    public float maxSlide = 1f;

    private Vector3 startPosition;
    private XRGrabInteractable grab;
    private Rigidbody rb;

    void Awake()
    {
        grab = GetComponent<XRGrabInteractable>();
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
        startPosition = transform.localPosition;

        // Freeze rotation so the chair doesn't tumble
        rb.freezeRotation = true;

        grab.selectExited.AddListener(OnReleased);
    }

    void OnDestroy()
    {
        grab.selectExited.RemoveListener(OnReleased);
    }

    void LateUpdate()
    {
        // Clamp position to the slide axis
        if (grab.isSelected)
        {
            Vector3 local = transform.localPosition;
            // Project onto slide axis relative to start
            float projected = Vector3.Dot(local - startPosition, slideAxis.normalized);
            projected = Mathf.Clamp(projected, minSlide, maxSlide);

            // Constrain to only move along the slide axis
            transform.localPosition = startPosition + slideAxis.normalized * projected;
            // Lock rotation
            transform.localRotation = Quaternion.identity;
        }
    }

    void OnReleased(SelectExitEventArgs args)
    {
        // Optional: snap to nearest slot when released
        // The ChairSlot trigger will handle detection
    }
}
```

**Key points:**
- `chairID` identifies each chair (you'll match these against the correct order).
- The `LateUpdate` clamp ensures the player can only slide the chair forward/backward, not sideways or up.
- Adjust `slideAxis`, `minSlide`, and `maxSlide` per chair depending on desk orientation.

---

## 2. Chair Slots (Snap Detection Zones)

Each desk gets an invisible trigger zone that detects which chair is parked there. Place these as child objects of each desk.

```csharp
using UnityEngine;

public class ChairSlot : MonoBehaviour
{
    [Header("Slot Identity")]
    [Tooltip("The position index of this slot (0, 1, 2, 3...)")]
    public int slotIndex;

    [Header("Reference")]
    public ChairPuzzleManager puzzleManager;

    // Which chair is currently in this slot (null if empty)
    [HideInInspector] public GrabbableChair currentChair;

    void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
    {
        var chair = other.GetComponentInParent<GrabbableChair>();
        if (chair != null)
        {
            currentChair = chair;
            puzzleManager.OnSlotUpdated();
        }
    }

    void OnTriggerExit(Collider other)
    {
        var chair = other.GetComponentInParent<GrabbableChair>();
        if (chair != null && chair == currentChair)
        {
            currentChair = null;
            puzzleManager.OnSlotUpdated();
        }
    }
}
```

**Scene setup for each slot:**
- Add an empty GameObject as a child of each desk.
- Add a **BoxCollider** (set `isTrigger = true`), sized to cover the chair-parking area.
- Attach `ChairSlot.cs` and assign the `slotIndex` (0, 1, 2, 3...) and reference to the `ChairPuzzleManager`.

---

## 3. Puzzle Manager (Check Order & Unlock)

This is the brain. It holds the correct arrangement and checks every time a chair enters or leaves a slot.

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Events;

public class ChairPuzzleManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    [Header("All slots in order (left to right, or however you define)")]
    public ChairSlot[] slots;

    [Header("Correct chair ID order (one per slot)")]
    [Tooltip("e.g. if slot 0 should have chair 3, slot 1 should have chair 1, etc.")]
    public int[] correctOrder;

    [Header("Events")]
    public UnityEvent onPuzzleSolved;
    public UnityEvent onPuzzleReset;

    private bool solved = false;

    public void OnSlotUpdated()
    {
        if (solved) return;

        if (CheckOrder())
        {
            solved = true;
            Debug.Log("Chair puzzle SOLVED! Code unlocked.");
            onPuzzleSolved?.Invoke();
        }
    }

    bool CheckOrder()
    {
        if (slots.Length != correctOrder.Length) return false;

        for (int i = 0; i < slots.Length; i++)
        {
            // Slot must have a chair, and it must be the correct one
            if (slots[i].currentChair == null) return false;
            if (slots[i].currentChair.chairID != correctOrder[i]) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    // Optional: call this to reset the puzzle
    public void ResetPuzzle()
    {
        solved = false;
        onPuzzleReset?.Invoke();
    }
}
```

**How the unlock works:**
- The `onPuzzleSolved` UnityEvent fires when all chairs are in the right slots. You can wire this in the Inspector to:
  - Reveal a code on a whiteboard/screen (enable a TextMeshPro object)
  - Open a locked door/drawer (play an animation or disable a collider)
  - Activate a keypad that was previously disabled
  - Play an audio cue

---

## 4. Scene Setup Checklist

Here's the step-by-step for wiring it up in Unity:

1. **Choose your chairs** — you have plenty of prefabs to pick from (e.g., from `Office Pack/Prefabs/Chairs/` or `school/Prefabs/props/`). Drag 3-4 different chairs into your `escape_room` scene.

2. **On each chair prefab:**
   - Add a **Rigidbody** (gravity on, not kinematic)
   - Add a **Collider** if not already present (mesh or box collider)
   - Add **`XRGrabInteractable`** component
   - Add **`GrabbableChair`** script, set a unique `chairID` (1, 2, 3, 4)
   - Tweak `slideAxis`, `minSlide`, `maxSlide` to match the desk orientation

3. **At each desk:**
   - Create an empty child GameObject (name it `ChairSlot_0`, `ChairSlot_1`, etc.)
   - Add a **BoxCollider** (`isTrigger = true`), position it where the chair should park
   - Add **`ChairSlot`** script, set the `slotIndex`

4. **Create a manager:**
   - Create an empty GameObject named `ChairPuzzleManager`
   - Add **`ChairPuzzleManager`** script
   - Drag all `ChairSlot` objects into the `slots` array (in order)
   - Set the `correctOrder` array (e.g., `[3, 1, 4, 2]`)
   - Wire `onPuzzleSolved` to whatever should happen (reveal code, open door, etc.)

5. **Link the slots** back to the manager (drag the manager into each slot's `puzzleManager` field).

---

## 5. Optional Enhancements

- **Visual hints**: Give each chair a distinct color or label (TextMeshPro on the backrest) so the player knows which is which. You could also put clues around the room (e.g., a note saying "Blue, Red, Green, Yellow").

- **Snap-to-slot**: When the player releases a chair near a slot, snap it to the exact position. Add this to `GrabbableChair.OnReleased`:

```csharp
void OnReleased(SelectExitEventArgs args)
{
    // Find nearest slot and snap
    ChairSlot nearest = FindNearestSlot();
    if (nearest != null && Vector3.Distance(transform.position, nearest.transform.position) < 0.5f)
    {
        transform.position = nearest.transform.position;
        rb.linearVelocity = Vector3.zero;
    }
}
```

- **Audio/visual feedback**: Play a click sound when a chair snaps into a slot, and a "success" jingle when the puzzle is solved.

- **Code display**: When solved, enable a GameObject with a TextMeshPro showing the unlock code (e.g., "4721") that the player then enters into a keypad elsewhere in the room.

All done, no lint errors. Here's what changed:

---

**Deleted** `ChairSlot.cs` — no longer needed since chairs stay parented to their desks.

**Rewrote `GrabbableChair.cs`** — Now works entirely in **local space** (respecting the parent desk). Key changes:
- The chair slides along a local axis between `pushedInOffset` and `pulledOutOffset` while grabbed.
- On release, it **snaps** to whichever end it's closer to (pushed in or pulled out).
- Sets `isPushedIn` accordingly and notifies the puzzle manager.

**Rewrote `ChairPuzzleManager.cs`** — Now tracks chairs directly instead of slots:
- Takes an array of `GrabbableChair` references and a matching `bool[] correctStates` (`true` = pushed in, `false` = pulled out).
- Every time a chair is released, it re-checks whether all chairs match the correct pattern.
- Fires `onPuzzleSolved` and optionally activates a `codeDisplay` GameObject when the combination is correct.

---

**How to wire it up in the scene:**

1. **On each chair** (child of its desk): Add `Rigidbody` + `XRGrabInteractable` + `GrabbableChair`. Set:
   - `chairIndex` — unique number for identification
   - `slideAxis` — the local direction toward/away from the desk (e.g. `(0, 0, 1)`)
   - `pushedInOffset` — `0` (at the starting position, tucked in)
   - `pulledOutOffset` — e.g. `0.5` (how far back the chair slides)
   - `puzzleManager` — drag in the manager object

2. **Manager** — Empty GameObject with `ChairPuzzleManager`. Drag all chairs into the `chairs` array, then set `correctStates` to the winning combination. For example with 4 chairs: `[true, false, false, true]` means chairs 0 and 3 pushed in, chairs 1 and 2 pulled out.

3. **Unlock action** — Wire `onPuzzleSolved` in the Inspector to reveal a code, open a door, play a sound, etc. Or drag a hidden TextMeshPro object into `codeDisplay` and it will auto-show when solved.

No errors. Here's the full step-by-step for setting everything up in the Unity Editor:

---

## Step 2 — Setting up the ChairPuzzleManager

1. In your `escape_room` scene Hierarchy, **right-click > Create Empty**. Name it `ChairPuzzleManager`.

2. In the Inspector, click **Add Component** and search for `Chair Puzzle Manager`. Attach it.

3. **Fill the `Chairs` array:**
   - Set the array size to however many chairs are in the puzzle (e.g. 4 if you have 2 desks with 2 chairs each).
   - Expand each desk in the Hierarchy, then **drag each chair** into the array slots. The order matters — it must match the `Correct States` array you set next.

4. **Fill the `Correct States` array:**
   - Set it to the same size as the Chairs array.
   - Check the box for chairs that should be **pushed in**, leave it unchecked for chairs that should be **pulled out**.
   - Example with 4 chairs: `[true, false, false, true]` means chairs 0 and 3 pushed in, chairs 1 and 2 pulled out.

5. **Link each chair back to the manager:**
   - Select each chair in the Hierarchy.
   - In its `GrabbableChair` component, drag the `ChairPuzzleManager` object into the **Puzzle Manager** field.

---

## Step 3 — Setting up the Water Bottle Unlock Effect

### A. Prepare the water bottle in the scene

1. If the water bottle isn't already in the scene, drag `Assets/Low Poly Cartoon Food and Groceries Pack/Prefabs/water_bottle.prefab` into the Hierarchy and position it where you want it.

2. Add the `WaterBottleUnlock` component to the water bottle (Add Component > search "Water Bottle Unlock").

### B. Add the glow light

1. **Right-click the water bottle** in the Hierarchy > **Light > Point Light**. This creates a Point Light as a child.
2. Position it roughly at the centre of the bottle (e.g. local position `0, 0.1, 0`).
3. **Uncheck the checkbox** at the top of the Inspector to **disable** it (it starts off and gets enabled by the script).
4. Back on the water bottle's `WaterBottleUnlock` component, drag this Point Light into the **Glow Light** field.
5. You can tweak `Glow Color` (default is a light blue) and `Glow Intensity` (default 3) in the Inspector to your liking.

### C. Add the floating text

1. **Right-click the water bottle** in the Hierarchy > **3D Object > Text - TextMeshPro**. (If Unity asks you to import TMP Essentials, click "Import" — you already have TextMesh Pro in the project so it should be fine.)
2. Position it above the bottle (e.g. local position `0, 0.2, 0`).
3. In the TextMeshPro component:
   - Set **Font Size** to something readable in VR (try `2`–`5`, adjust by testing).
   - Set **Alignment** to Center / Middle.
   - Optionally change the font color to match your glow.
4. **Disable the GameObject** (uncheck the checkbox at the top of the Inspector).
5. Drag it into the `WaterBottleUnlock` component's **Unlock Text** field.
6. The `Message` field defaults to `"the curse is lifted"` — change it if you want.

### D. Wire the puzzle to the bottle

1. Select the `ChairPuzzleManager` object in the Hierarchy.
2. In the Inspector, find the **On Puzzle Solved** event.
3. Click the **+** button to add an entry.
4. Drag the **water bottle** (the one with `WaterBottleUnlock` on it) into the object field.
5. From the function dropdown, choose **WaterBottleUnlock > Unlock()**.

---

That's it. When the player gets all the chairs into the correct pushed-in / pulled-out pattern, the manager fires `onPuzzleSolved`, which calls `Unlock()` on the water bottle — the light fades in with a glow and the text "the curse is lifted" floats up above the bottle.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The chairs disappearing is almost certainly caused by the **Rigidbody with gravity** on child objects. When a chair is a child of a desk:

1. Unity physics doesn't handle nested Rigidbodies well — a Rigidbody on a child object will fight with the parent's transform
2. Gravity pulls the chair down, but since we're controlling position in `LateUpdate` only when grabbed, the un-grabbed chair with gravity enabled falls through the floor

The fix is to make the Rigidbody **kinematic**. Since we manually control position in `LateUpdate` and `OnReleased`, we don't need physics simulation at all. 

The XRGrabInteractable still needs a Rigidbody present, but kinematic ones work fine — I just need to set the movement type appropriately. There's also a potential issue in the offset calculation where if `pushedInOffset` is 0 but `startPushedIn` is true, any non-zero offset will shift the chair from its editor position, which could explain the disappearing behavior.

I should make the Rigidbody kinematic, set the XRGrabInteractable to use Instantaneous movement, and reconsider how the initial position logic works. ### Chair disappearing fix

The problem was that the Rigidbody on each chair had gravity enabled and wasn't kinematic. Since chairs are **child objects** of desks, a non-kinematic Rigidbody fights with the parent transform — physics pulls the chair downward and it falls through the desk/floor. The fix in `GrabbableChair.cs`:

- **`rb.isKinematic = true`** — physics engine won't simulate gravity or collisions on the chair
- **`rb.useGravity = false`** — belt-and-suspenders, explicitly off
- **`grab.movementType = Instantaneous`** — tells XRI to move the object directly (required for kinematic bodies)

All chair movement is now controlled entirely by the script, so there's nothing for physics to interfere with.

Also make sure that in the Unity Inspector, each chair's Rigidbody has **Is Kinematic** checked and **Use Gravity** unchecked (the script forces this at runtime, but it's good practice to match in the editor too).

---

### Quit Button

Created `QuitButton.cs`. To set it up in your scene:

1. **Create a world-space UI Canvas:**
   - Hierarchy > right-click > **UI > Canvas**
   - In the Canvas component, set **Render Mode** to **World Space**
   - Scale it down (e.g. `0.002, 0.002, 0.002`) and position it on a wall, near a door, or wherever makes sense

2. **Add a Button:**
   - Right-click the Canvas > **UI > Button - TextMeshPro**
   - Change the button text to "Quit" or "Exit"
   - Style it however you like (color, size, font)

3. **Wire it up:**
   - Add the `QuitButton` component to the Button (or the Canvas, doesn't matter)
   - On the Button's **On Click()** event, click **+**, drag in the object with `QuitButton`, and select **QuitButton > QuitGame()**

4. **Make it pokeable in VR:**
   - Add an **XR Simple Interactable** or **XR Poke Interactable** component to the Button so the player can press it with their VR hand/controller
   - Alternatively, if you already have ray interactors set up, the standard UI Button will work with XR ray interaction on a world-space canvas automatically

In the Editor it stops Play mode; in a build it exits the application.

_**Agent (model default, mode Agent)**_

Since you already have ray interactors, the standard Unity UI Button on a world-space Canvas will just work out of the box with XRI — no extra poke/interactable components needed. Here's how it works:

---

### How XR Ray + World-Space UI works

XRI includes a component called **Tracked Device Graphics Raycaster** (replaces the regular `Graphic Raycaster` that Canvas normally uses). This lets the XR ray interactor interact with standard Unity UI elements (buttons, toggles, sliders, etc.) the same way a mouse would on a screen-space canvas.

### What you need to do

1. **Create the Canvas:**
   - Hierarchy > right-click > **UI > Canvas**
   - Set **Render Mode** to **World Space**
   - Scale it down so it's a reasonable size in VR (try `0.001, 0.001, 0.001` and adjust)
   - Position and rotate it where you want (e.g. on a wall near the exit)

2. **Swap the Raycaster:**
   - On the Canvas object, **remove** the default `Graphic Raycaster` component (right-click it > Remove Component)
   - Click **Add Component** and search for **Tracked Device Graphic Raycaster** — add that instead
   - This is the key step — it tells Unity "let XR rays hit this canvas"

3. **Add the Button:**
   - Right-click the Canvas > **UI > Button - TextMeshPro**
   - Change the button label to "Quit" or "Exit Game"

4. **Wire the quit action:**
   - Add the `QuitButton` component to any object (the Button itself is fine)
   - On the Button's **On Click()** event in the Inspector, click **+**
   - Drag the object with `QuitButton` into the object field
   - From the dropdown, select **QuitButton > QuitGame()**

### How it works at runtime

- Your XR ray interactor (the laser pointer from your controller) naturally hits the **Tracked Device Graphic Raycaster** on the Canvas
- When the ray hovers over the Button, it highlights (just like a mouse hover)
- When you pull the trigger/select, it fires the Button's **On Click()** event
- That calls `QuitGame()`, which exits the app

No extra scripts, no poke interactable, no XR Simple Interactable — the ray interactor + Tracked Device Graphic Raycaster handle all the UI interaction automatically. The only thing people usually forget is step 2 (swapping the raycaster), so make sure you do that.

No lint errors. Here's what was changed and what you need to do:

---

### Chairs fix (code change)

`GrabbableChair.cs` now has an `EnsureColliderExists()` method that runs in `Awake`. It:

1. Checks if any collider exists on the chair or its children
2. If not, it computes a bounding box from all the mesh renderers and auto-adds a `BoxCollider` that wraps the whole chair
3. Logs a message to the Console so you can see it working

This should make the chairs immediately grabbable on your next build. You'll see `[GrabbableChair] Auto-added BoxCollider to 'ChairName'` in the Console if it had to create one.

If you'd rather add colliders manually (for tighter fit), you can add a `BoxCollider` or `MeshCollider` to each chair in the Inspector yourself — the script will detect the existing collider and skip the auto-add.

---

### Quit button fix (scene setup — no code change needed)

The `QuitButton.cs` script is fine. The issue is that XR ray interactors can't interact with standard Unity UI unless two things are in place:

**1. On your Canvas object:**
- Select the Canvas in the Hierarchy
- **Remove** the `Graphic Raycaster` component (right-click > Remove Component)
- **Add** `Tracked Device Graphic Raycaster` instead (Add Component > search for it)

**2. On your EventSystem object:**
- Find the `EventSystem` in the Hierarchy (it was auto-created with the Canvas)
- Check if it has a `Standalone Input Module` — if so, **remove it**
- **Add** `XR UI Input Module` (Add Component > search for it)
- This replaces mouse/keyboard input with XR controller input for UI

After those two changes, your XR ray should be able to hover and click the Quit button like it does with everything else in the scene.

Your project is using the **XRI Default Input Actions** from the Starter Assets. Based on those bindings, here's what grabs objects:

### Grab / Select — **Grip button** (side squeeze)

The "Select" action (which is what `XRGrabInteractable` listens to) is bound to:

- **Controller**: `{GripButton}` — the **side grip/squeeze button** on your controller (the button on the side you press with your middle finger, not the trigger)
- **Hand tracking**: `graspFirm` / pinch gesture

So to grab a chair (or the water bottle, or anything with `XRGrabInteractable`):

1. **Point your ray** at the chair (or get your hand close for direct grab)
2. **Squeeze the grip button** (side of the controller) to grab
3. **Release the grip** to let go

The **trigger** (index finger button) is bound to the "Activate" action, which is a secondary action while holding — it doesn't grab by itself.

### For the Quit button (UI)

UI interaction (clicking buttons on a world-space Canvas) uses the same approach — point the ray at the button and **squeeze the grip** or **pull the trigger** depending on your `XR UI Input Module` settings. With the default XRI setup, **both** grip and trigger typically work for UI selection, but the trigger is the more common one for UI clicks.

**Quick summary:**
- **Grab objects**: Grip button (side squeeze)
- **Click UI buttons**: Trigger (index finger) while pointing the ray at the button

If you're on a Meta Quest controller specifically, the grip is the button your middle/ring finger naturally rests on along the side of the controller.

No lint errors. Here's what the update fixes:

---

### Problem 1: XRI didn't know about the collider

`XRGrabInteractable` collects its collider list in its own `Awake()`. Since Unity doesn't guarantee `Awake()` order between components on the same object, the grab interactable may have initialized **before** our script added the BoxCollider — so it had an empty collider list and was invisible to rays.

**Fix:** After ensuring a collider exists, the script now **force-refreshes** the grab interactable's collider list:

```csharp
grab.colliders.Clear();
foreach (Collider col in allColliders)
    grab.colliders.Add(col);
```

### Problem 2: Desk collider blocking the ray

Since chairs are children of desks, and the desks likely have colliders, the XR ray hits the desk first. The desk isn't an interactable, so the ray just stops there — it never reaches the chair behind it.

**Fix:** The new `ExcludeParentDesksFromRaycast()` method walks up the parent hierarchy and moves any colliders on parent objects (the desk) to the **"Ignore Raycast"** layer. This makes the ray pass through the desk and reach the chair. It only does this for parents that don't have their own `XRBaseInteractable`, so it won't break other interactive objects.

Here's what changed and why:

### Root cause

The line `grab.movementType = XRBaseInteractable.MovementType.Instantaneous` was likely a **compile error** in XRI 3.3.1 — that enum lives on `XRGrabInteractable`, not `XRBaseInteractable`. When a script has a compile error in Unity, the **entire script silently doesn't run** — no errors in the headset, the object just sits there with no behavior. That means:
- No collider was ever added
- No parent layers were changed
- The `XRGrabInteractable` had an empty collider list (as confirmed in the scene file)
- The ray had nothing to hit

### What the rewrite fixes

1. **Removed the `MovementType` line entirely** — the default movement type works fine; no need to set it in code and risk a compile error.

2. **Moved all setup to `Start()` instead of `Awake()`** — this guarantees `XRGrabInteractable` has fully initialized (its `Awake()` and `OnEnable()` are done) before we touch it.

3. **After adding colliders, toggles the interactable off/on** — this forces XRI's interaction manager to **unregister and re-register** the interactable with the fresh collider list. Without this, the interaction manager wouldn't know about our newly added colliders.

4. **Debug logging at every step** — you should now see messages in the Console like:
   - `[GrabbableChair] Auto-added BoxCollider to 'ChairName'`
   - `[GrabbableChair] 'ChairName' registered 1 collider(s) with XRGrabInteractable`
   - `[GrabbableChair] Set parent 'DeskName' to Ignore Raycast layer`

   If you DON'T see these messages, the script still isn't running and there's another compile error to track down.

Try building again — the ray should now detect and highlight the chairs.

No lint errors. Here's what changed:

### The problem

`XRGrabInteractable` was trying to move the chair to your hand every frame (that's what it does — it makes grabbed objects follow the controller). Our `LateUpdate` was then fighting to snap it back to the slide axis. Two systems wrestling over the same transform = warping.

### The fix

Three key changes:

**1. Disabled XRI's built-in movement:**
```csharp
grab.trackPosition = false;
grab.trackRotation = false;
grab.throwOnDetach = false;
```
Now XRI only handles **grab detection** (ray highlight, grip to select). It no longer moves the chair at all.

**2. Track hand movement ourselves on grab:**
When you grab the chair, the script records where your hand is and where the chair is. Each frame while grabbed, it computes how far your hand has moved in world space, projects that movement onto the slide axis, and applies only that component to the chair's local position.

**3. Smooth 1:1 sliding:**
If you move your hand 10cm along the slide direction, the chair moves 10cm. Movement perpendicular to the slide axis is ignored. The chair stays locked to its rotation and can only slide between `pushedInOffset` and `pulledOutOffset`.

The behavior should now be: point the ray, grip to grab, move your hand forward/backward to slide the chair, release to snap it to pushed-in or pulled-out.

_**Agent (model default, mode Agent)**_

Yes, the snapping is already implemented. When you release the grip, `OnReleased` fires and does this:

```97:109:/Users/kvg2005/Documents/GitHub/CS417/MP1/Assets/scripts/GrabbableChair.cs
    void OnReleased(SelectExitEventArgs args)
    {
        Vector3 localOffset = transform.localPosition - localStartPos;
        float projected = Vector3.Dot(localOffset, slideDir);

        float midpoint = (pushedInOffset + pulledOutOffset) * 0.5f;
        isPushedIn = projected < midpoint;

        float snapOffset = isPushedIn ? pushedInOffset : pulledOutOffset;
        transform.localPosition = localStartPos + slideDir * snapOffset;
        transform.localRotation = localStartRot;

        if (puzzleManager != null)
            puzzleManager.OnChairStateChanged();
    }
```

It calculates the midpoint between pushed-in and pulled-out, then snaps the chair to whichever end it's closer to. So if you drag the chair past halfway and let go, it snaps to pulled-out. If it's still in the first half, it snaps back to pushed-in.

**How visible the snap is depends on your offset values.** Right now `pushedInOffset` defaults to `0` and `pulledOutOffset` defaults to `0.5` (half a meter). So the two positions are only 0.5m apart. If that doesn't feel like a clear enough difference in your scene, increase `pulledOutOffset` in the Inspector on each chair — try `1.0` or `1.5` for a more dramatic pulled-out position. You can tweak it per-chair to match the desk depth.

In short: yes, the snap works as-is. If it doesn't feel distinct enough visually, just increase `pulledOutOffset` on each chair in the Inspector.
